title: Learn to do well (Isaiah 1:16–17)
hook: "cease to do evil; learn to do well; seek justice, relieve the oppressed"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word navi, and your line: a prophet speaks to now. Today the book of Isaiah opens, and it speaks to now from its very first chapter.

The first word of the book in Hebrew is chazon, a vision. "The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz." And the vision doesn't begin with angels or the future. It begins almost like a courtroom. Heaven and earth are called to listen. The people have brought offerings, kept new moons and festivals, filled the courts of the Temple. And God, through Isaiah, says: I'm tired of it. When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes. Why? Your hands are full of blood.
screen: `CHAZON: A VISION.` → `HEAR, O HEAVENS.` → `YOUR HANDS ARE FULL OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Then comes the turn, a list of verbs. "Wash you, make you clean," it begins: put your evil doings away from God's sight. Then: "Cease to do evil; Learn to do well; Seek justice, relieve the oppressed, Judge the fatherless, plead for the widow." The Hebrew word behind justice is mishpat, which can also mean judgment. Notice three things. First, the order: wash, then stop, then learn. Stopping the harm comes before anything else, but stopping isn't the end. Second, the verb in the middle: learn. Doing well isn't described as a feeling or an instinct. It's learned, like a language or a trade. You can be bad at it at first, and practice. Third, how concrete it gets. Not be a good person in general: the fatherless, the widow, the oppressed. These are the people the verse names, and its verb for the widow is plead: take up her case. And the complaint about offerings? The text gives the reason: hands full of blood, raised in prayer. Worship alongside cruelty. Jewish tradition reads this chapter as the haftarah on the Shabbat before Tisha B'Av, and that Sabbath takes its name from the book's first word: Shabbat Chazon, the Sabbath of the vision. Right before the day of mourning for the Temple, Jews hear the prophet's call to wash, cease and learn.
screen: `WASH YOU, MAKE YOU CLEAN.` · `CEASE TO DO EVIL.` · then, large: `LEARN TO DO WELL.` · then: `THE FATHERLESS AND THE WIDOW.` · `SHABBAT CHAZON.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little and ask Isaiah's question: who near me has no one pleading their case? A neighbor whose landlord won't answer, a coworker being talked over, a kid on the edge of the group. Hold that one person or need in mind, and if you pray, ask for mishpat, to learn to do well.
Mishpat, the Hebrew word for justice, part of Isaiah's call to wash, cease doing evil, learn to do well, and plead for the widow and the fatherless.
Your line: stopping isn't the end. Doing well is learned, one case at a time. That's day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Isaiah chapter 1 is read in the synagogue as the haftarah on Shabbat Chazon, the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, named for the chapter's first word.
